title_original: ‘You Can See Everything’ Review: The Eyes Have It
excerpt_original: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s metatextual portrait of the disgraced Elizabeth Holmes is a work of genius that asks how we can ever know anything – truth, language, love – at all

blocks.text: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s metatextual portrait of the disgraced Elizabeth Holmes is a work of genius that asks how we can ever know anything – truth, language, love – at all. Spoilers ahead.

‘Everything I had ever been told’, Joan Didion writes in The White Album (1979), on the subject of her 1968 nervous breakdown, ‘insisted that the production was never meant to be improvised: I was supposed to have a script, and had mislaid it. I was supposed to hear cues, and no longer did.’ The ‘production’ in question was everyday life outside of her professional persona – the messy, quotidian business of parenthood; of marriage; of making small talk with the neighbours, and so on. I thought about this while watching season one of The Rehearsal , the HBO series created by comedian, writer, director and amateur magician Nathan Fielder, whose own sense of having mislaid the proverbial script seemed to have driven him insane. The show’s mindfuck of a premise – that if every part of human existence could be staged and meticulously rehearsed, it would eradicate all possibility of failure – took the idea of life as a production and ran with it, first using test subjects recruited on Craigslist and then later shifting focus to Fielder, who became part of an ersatz family set-up: a farm with its own false, accelerated seasons; a stranger for a wife; a son named Adam, like the very first man, who was played by a series of actors in line with child labour laws. The more baroque and Kaufmanesque these ‘rehearsals’ for marriage and fatherhood became, the more frustration Fielder felt. “I was starting to wonder how I could so easily create feelings inside other people’s rehearsals,” he lamented, “when I couldn’t do it for myself.”

The reason for Fielder’s dilemma is that while we are capable of lying to ourselves, it still takes another party to truly deceive us – to catch us completely by surprise, and to administer the jolt of mysterious electricity which can turn into love or fascination; to hand us a brand-new script, and recruit us as players in their own grand production. In You Can See Everything , a three-hour documentary-drama following disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in her last month of freedom before incarceration, Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim are given the gift of total access to one of the twenty-first century’s most famous liars. Better yet, another less famous liar is thrown in as a bonus: Holmes’s partner, an unctuous and volatile man named Billy Evans, is duplicitous, quietly coercive and horribly arrogant. The two bill and coo over each other, and claim to be working on an adaptation of the Theranos brand – news which will no doubt alarm those viewers familiar with the details of her court case . Holmes insists on her innocence, in spite of her conviction. They have two small children, one of whom is mere weeks old, and our first sight of Holmes is a shot of her cradling the infant, framed by the bars of his crib. It is a dark joke about her forthcoming imprisonment, and one which reflects the film’s tonal ricochet between thriller and terribly black comedy. (When Fielder, who is staying in their home, first appears onscreen, he is looming at the window like a scruffy Canadian Nosferatu.) The picture is also a work of two halves: first a documentary, then a mad, metatextual joyride through truth and performance, fiction and fact.

blocks.text: As in Oppenheim’s other 2026 directorial outing, Primetime , close-ups are frequently used as a tool to stoke anxiety, but also to remind us that even if the eyes are a window to the soul, there are those walking among us who have chosen to figuratively tint them. At times, these close-ups recall a later scene from The Rehearsal – in which Fielder pays a visit to the Center for Autism & Related Disorders and takes a pictorial test called ‘Reading the Mind in the Eyes’. There, we watch Fielder examine a series of tightly-framed photographs of eyes, trying to parse whether each connotes “anger” or “sadness” or “joy”. You Can See Everything poses a similar kind of visual test; it is a magic-eye picture, appearing to be several things at once. The camera seems to be trying to get inside the skulls of its subjects, until the very pores of their poker-faces fill up the screen. Here, in Fielder and Holmes, are two of the most notably manipulative figures in recent American history, each with an uncanny ability to play at being naïve and an inhuman tolerance for shame. In the film’s second half, Fielder invokes a particular trick by the famous street illusionist David Blaine. (‘Illusionist’ being, in its own way, a synonym for ‘fraud’.) Blaine, he explains, would amaze his subjects by puncturing his hand with an ice pick. In spite of the fact that it looked like magic, he was actually doing it, having drilled a hole in his hand for the pick to pass through. Holmes, Fielder posits, is a little like Blaine: a prankster muddling the possible with the impossible, then wrongfooting us as to which is which. Coming from Fielder, who has made a career out of doing the same, it is certainly a compliment – like finding like, in a manner both compelling and perverse.

blocks.caption: You Can See Everything , dir. Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, 2026. Courtesy A24

blocks.text: If you have not yet seen the film, you have at least seen the two-frame meme: Fielder sits opposite Holmes on the couch, their faces close enough to kiss. “Why would I deceive you?” Holmes asks him, with an unblinking, Bambi-in-psychosis expression on her face. He stares back, dumbstruck; somewhere out there in the real world, the finger of a monkey’s paw curls. A screenshot of Fielder in this moment has taken on a life of its own in those online circles in which he has, a little unexpectedly, been crowned a sex symbol, and it’s true there is a touch of something tender in his gaze. Still, I do not think we are seeing lust, exactly, or love, in spite of what certain critics and online commenters have suggested. We are seeing curiousness, amazement, perhaps even relief. Nathan Fielder is about to get everything he wants, which is to say he is about to be thoroughly Fieldered: subjected to the same kind of world-scrambling, mind-melting puppetry he usually performs on others, the result being that even if he cannot quite see everything, he certainly feels something.

blocks.caption: You Can See Everything , dir. Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, 2026. Courtesy A24

blocks.text: Once Holmes disappears from the film, now incarcerated, Fielder and Oppenheim must of course find a replacement. Happily, one soon arrives, in the form of the very funny, very smart, faintly bonkers Hollywood star Amanda Seyfried, who played Holmes to Emmy-winning effect in The Dropout (2022). Scottie , do you believe that someone out of the past – someone out of a Hulu miniseries – can enter and take possession of a living being? Such a possession is usually referred to as ‘acting’. (‘Actor’ being, in its own way, a synonym for ‘fraud’.) A dizzying scene in which Seyfried watches Holmes watching The Dropout proves to be one of the best in the movie; thrilling, too, is her first viewing of Fielder’s latest footage of Holmes, during which she becomes newly alive and alert, muscle memory kicking back into gear. It is obvious that just as Fielder – a director of behaviour by nature – is delighted to sit back for a change and be the subject of Holmes’s control, Seyfried aches to slip back into her skin. She enters in seamlessly, as if no time had passed; she has Holmes’s great Margaret Keane eyes and her colouring, and to this she adds her eerie intensity; when we are watching her acting out reported conversations and memories that Fielder has provided for her, we barely see Amanda Seyfried at all. You Can See Everything is filled with discussions about the specifics of language – whether “can” means “is capable of”, whether a quotation from an interview ought to read “I” or “they”, and so on – and such discussions are also required whenever an actor is being directed from a script. Fielder coaches Seyfried to make her more and more like the object of his strange fascination, and Seyfried meets his efforts with a conspiratorial smirk. Both know what it is like to devote themselves to Holmes, and to be drawn in by her freaky tractor beam. Both, too, are protective of her – in the human sense that they pity her a little, absolutely, but also in the cynical way that an artist is possessive and secretive about a pet subject.

blocks.text: Funny, really, that we talk about falling for a person, but we also say we’ve fallen for a scam, or a lie. In spite of being damaged, toxic people, Holmes and Evans do seem to be in love, as demonstrated by Seyfried’s recreation of the now-imprisoned fraudster’s final conversation with Fielder: as Holmes, she admits that where she once imagined God as an organising force, she now sees Billy as her purpose, and the “monuments of love” that they build to each other as her most vital work. The film ends with Fielder looking on through the fence of the prison as the couple and their children play outside in the yard, just like the kind of all-American family he tried to create for himself in The Rehearsal . The New Yorker ’s Richard Brody says something truly beautiful about this last scene: that the film ends up resembling ‘an equation that proves the existence of love’. This is not to say that Oppenheim and Fielder show all of the work, since whatever the parts of this equation might be, they are as slippery and ineffable as language. The phrases ‘to be loved is to be seen’ and ‘to be loved is to be known’ are often used interchangeably in pop-psych babble, and yet it is obvious that ‘seeing’ and ‘knowing’ are not quite the same thing. There is deceit at the heart of seduction, and though we might see everything of someone, there is no one on earth who can know everything about another individual, with their singular wants, needs, fears and perversions. Love is truly a high-risk activity, and there is not yet a machine that can confirm for us whether or not someone will destroy us, disease-like, in the end.

If one thing mars this otherwise genius film, it is a brief and peculiar moment of incuriosity from Fielder, who asks Holmes’s father when all of the trouble began. “Oh, that’s easy,” he replies matter-of-factly. “When she was 19, she was raped.” If the word ‘can’ is flexible, the word ‘rape’ is not. The statement passes unexamined in spite of its obvious relevance. You Can See Everything is careful to avoid making definitive judgements about Holmes’s state of mind; it is not a work of investigative journalism, rather an artwork about the subjectivity of truth, the unreliability of memory, and so on. Nevertheless, I kept thinking about Holmes’s father’s comment after leaving the screening. Here was an event that might have cracked open a person enough to make them not just duplicitous, but capable of living in an alternate reality: one in which conceptions of correctness and innocence were paramount, even as this individual made a bad sequence of decisions, some illegal, some immoral, all dangerous. It might also lead a woman to adopt the baritone voice and the buttoned-up style of a powerful man for self-protection, as Holmes did. Who can know? Not me, not you, not Fielder or Oppenheim. Perhaps not even Holmes. Not long before she leaves for jail, Fielder jokes that she should have simply said that Theranos was a bit, since this is how he has got away with so much amoral trickery in the past. Holmes, who claims to be a literal thinker, replies that what she did was not a joke. Perhaps a part of her, now, wishes that it had been. What was it that Marx said about Napoleon Bonaparte? History repeats itself: ‘the first time as tragedy, the second time as farce’.
